paras: The Barbour County whitecapping was a campaign of threats and night attacks by a band of white men, called whitecaps, against Black residents of one part of Barbour County, Alabama, in the summer of 1903. Reports said Black laborers were driven off several large plantations and warned to leave under penalty of death, and a federal prosecutor described one man being beaten and lashed. The case led to arrests by federal officers, guilty pleas to assault and battery in the county court, and six federal conspiracy indictments in January 1904.

According to the federal prosecutor, between the last of July and the middle of August 1903 a group of men without warrant or legal authority came at night to the house of Marion Shipman, "a reputable negro of family," presumably looking for an alleged murderer, and Shipman helped them search.

Several days later, between 3 and 4 a.m., the men returned, and when Shipman refused to admit them they battered down his door. Shipman knocked one of them down, but he was seized, bound, gagged, beaten with a pistol and a gun, taken several miles down a road and lashed.

By August 20 a "well authenticated rumor" had reached Montgomery of "a practical race war" in one portion of Barbour, with Black residents being driven from the county by whitecaps. The labor on three or more large plantations was said to have been run off, and labor in that section was described as badly demoralized. Later reports said the gang had for some time warned Black residents to leave "under penalty of death."

A prominent Barbour citizen went to Montgomery to ask U.S. District Judge Thomas G. Jones how the whitecapping could be stopped. Jones reportedly referred him to the governor, saying federal authorities should not be called on "to do what the state authorities ought to do." With Governor Jelks away, his private secretary promised to lay the facts before him, and a wire report noted that Barbour was the governor's own county and that he was expected to investigate.

Federal officers moved instead: by August 28 U.S. deputy J. F. Greene was in Barbour with warrants for "some prominent people." On September 15 seven Barbour men were brought before U.S. Commissioner Tutwiler at Troy and jailed pending hearings, and five of them were later held in $500 bond each.

On January 16, 1904, the grand jury indicted six white men of Zeiglers post office, Beat 8, for conspiring to intimidate Albert Barefield, Marion Shipman, Hillard Turner and Nancy Miles in the exercise of their constitutional rights. Judge Jones told the five arraigned that their earlier prosecution in the state courts for assault and battery on one victim was no bar to the federal charge. Although it had been indicated that all five would plead guilty, one declared he "jés naturally ain't guilty," the others nodded, and all were released on bond pending a hearing. No report of the outcome of the federal case was found.

The episode was covered only by white papers, first as a one-line "race war" item in the Birmingham Age-Herald and then in a Montgomery special printed by the Atlanta Constitution under the headline "White Caps Scare Negroes." These reports treated the expulsions chiefly as a labor problem and repeated, without a source, that Black residents' "overt acts" had caused the outbreak. The September arrest story ran in Louisville, Indianapolis and Atlanta, and the Indianapolis Journal called the accused "Night Riders."

The bond item, printed in Birmingham, Atlanta and two Southern weeklies, described the accused as "prominent citizens." The Montgomery Advertiser headed a section of its indictment story "Persecuted Negroes" and gave the prosecutor's account of Shipman's beating in detail, yet said there was "not a bad face among the five men." The local Clayton Record answered that the Advertiser's account created an unjustified impression, that the affair was "not so bad as it would seem," and that the men had "had punishment enough."
Accounts differ on the cause: an unattributed August report blamed "overt acts" of Black residents, while the prosecutor said the men first came looking for an alleged murderer.

bases: Every report calls the perpetrators whitecaps or whitecappers who drove Black tenants and laborers off plantations by threats and night visits, and the men were indicted federally for 'whitecapping' (A3, A8, A18).

Independent Montgomery specials (A3, A7), a Troy wire on the arrests (A8), a federal grand jury indictment with the prosecutor's statement in court (A18), and the local Clayton Record, which disputes only the seriousness, all report the whitecapping (A19, A20).

accounts.gist: A 'well authenticated rumor' of a 'practical race war' in part of Barbour, with Black laborers run off three or more large plantations; the cause was said to be 'overt acts' of Black residents who had made themselves 'obnoxious'.

accounts.label: Troy wire on the arrests
accounts.gist: The men brought before the commissioner were alleged members of a gang that had for some time terrorized Barbour's Black residents, warning them to leave on pain of death.

accounts.label: Federal prosecutor
accounts.gist: The men came to Marion Shipman's house at night without a warrant, presumably hunting an alleged murderer; days later they battered down his door, bound, gagged and beat him and lashed him several miles away.

accounts.label: Defendant
accounts.gist: At arraignment one defendant said he was 'naturally' not guilty and the others nodded.

accounts.label: Clayton Record (local)
accounts.gist: The Advertiser's account gave an unjustified impression; the affair was 'not so bad', some men had already pleaded guilty to assault and battery in the county court, and they had been punished enough.

framing.detail: August reports framed the episode as a labor problem ('Labor in Barbour County ... Is Badly Demoralized', 'White Caps Scare Negroes') and passed on, unattributed, the claim that Black residents' 'overt acts' caused it.
September wire items called the accused 'alleged whitecappers' and 'prominent citizens'; the Indianapolis Journal headed its copy 'Arrest of Night Riders for Terrorizing Blacks'.

The Montgomery Advertiser headlined 'Persecuted Negroes' and printed the prosecutor's 'remarkable statements', while describing the defendants as having 'not a bad face' among them and mocking one's dialect.
The Clayton Record, the local paper, said the affair was 'not so bad as it would seem' and pleaded for leniency, while saying it did not condone the crime.

info: Prosecutor placed the attacks on Marion Shipman between the last of July and the middle of August 1903; whitecapping first reported in Montgomery on Aug. 20-21, 1903.
One portion of Barbour County; the indicted men were from Zeiglers post office, Beat 8.
Black residents and plantation laborers in part of Barbour County; the indictments named Albert Barefield, Marion Shipman, Hillard Turner and Nancy Miles.

No crime was charged against the victims; a Montgomery special said the outbreak was 'said to be due to some overt acts of the negroes' who had made themselves 'obnoxious'; the prosecutor said the men first came to Shipman's house presumably searching for an alleged murderer.

A 'gang' of white Barbour County men described as whitecaps; named in arrests and indictments as John Green, Jesse Green, James (Jim) Sanders, Buford McCall, Richard Mann, A. V. Norton, Wash Green, Morgan Padgett and Richard Knowles.

Five men were arraigned; it was first indicated all would plead guilty, but one declared himself not guilty and the others nodded; all were released on bonds with a hearing set for Thursday. No report of the federal verdict or sentence was found.
